# Script to generate the results for the manuscript figures, tables, text for the field paper, and supplementary materials

Published: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1618866726005194

D.M. Jaeger, J.M Friedman, M.P. Paulsen, B.M. Miller, K.N. Suding, T.R. Seastedt, C.A. Wessman,
Budburst in the city: Urbanization-induced differences in leaf and flower emergence in Boulder, Colorado,
Urban Forestry & Urban Greening, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ufug.2026.129779.

# Last updated in Sep 2026 dataset following reviewer suggestions that keeps phenology separated by year and tree, so those can be random effects.

# 3.1 Intra-urban phenological variation 
```{r - julian-day-results}
# load data
pheno.f <- read.csv("data/field-data-2019-2021/field-data-by-site-all_phenophase_by_site_jul_and_dep.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# filter to just leaf open and flower emerge
pheno.f.lo.ft <- pheno.f %>%
  filter(phenophase == "leafopen" | phenophase == "floweremerge")

# 2020 julian day range - leaves
pheno.f.lo.ft %>% 
  filter(year == "2020", phenophase == "leafopen") %>% 
  summarize(jul.min = min(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE), jul.max = max(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE), jul.var = max(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE)-min(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE), total.var = max(pheno_dep_l50_f20, na.rm = TRUE)-min(pheno_dep_l50_f20, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% View()


# 2021 julian day range - flowers

pheno.f.lo.ft %>% 
  filter(year == "2021", phenophase == "floweremerge") %>% 
  summarize(jul.min = min(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE), jul.max = max(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE), jul.var = max(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE)-min(jul0.5_0.2, na.rm = TRUE), total.var = max(pheno_dep_l50_f20, na.rm = TRUE)-min(pheno_dep_l50_f20, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% View()

# average range - leaves
  # Which site had the earliest leaf emergence on average
pheno.f.lo.ft %>% 
  filter(year == "average", phenophase == "leafopen") %>% 
 slice(which.min(jul0.5_0.2))  %>% View() # CUNO earliest

 # Which site had the latest leaf emergence on average
pheno.f.lo.ft %>% 
  filter(year == "average", phenophase == "leafopen") %>% 
 slice(which.max(jul0.5_0.2))  %>% View() # NOBO latest



# average range - flowers

  # Which site had the earliest flower emergence on average
pheno.f.lo.ft %>% 
  filter(year == "average", phenophase == "floweremerge") %>% 
 slice(which.min(jul0.5_0.2))  %>% View() # 14ST earliest

 # Which site had the latest flower emergence on average
pheno.f.lo.ft %>% 
  filter(year == "average", phenophase == "floweremerge") %>% 
 slice(which.max(jul0.5_0.2))  %>% View() # THU2 latest
```

```{r average-annual-temp}
  mutate(year= "2019")


# Jan 2020 - May 2020
t.2020 <- bt.dat.month.dep.s %>%
  filter(year == 2020, month < 6) %>% 
  dplyr::select(month, year, sensor_name8, mean_tempC:max_tempC) %>% 
  summarise(meanC = mean(mean_tempC, na.rm = T), mean_sd = sd(mean_tempC, na.rm = T), minC = mean(min_tempC, na.rm = T), min_sd = sd(min_tempC, na.rm = T), maxC = mean(max_tempC, na.rm = T), max_sd = sd(max_tempC, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  mutate(year= "2020")

# Jan 2021 - May 2021
t.2021 <- bt.dat.month.dep.s %>%
  filter(year == 2021, month < 6) %>% 
  dplyr::select(month, year, sensor_name8, mean_tempC:max_tempC) %>% 
 summarise(meanC = mean(mean_tempC, na.rm = T), mean_sd = sd(mean_tempC, na.rm = T), minC = mean(min_tempC, na.rm = T), min_sd = sd(min_tempC, na.rm = T), maxC = mean(max_tempC, na.rm = T), max_sd = sd(max_tempC, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  mutate(year= "2021")

# bind table
annual_temps <- rbind(t.2019, t.2020, t.2021)

write.csv(annual_temps, "data/outputs/annual_temps/annual_temps_study_period.csv")
```

# 3.2 Predictors of tree phenology
## Intra-urban temperature relationship with phenology 

```{r LMM leaves - temp}

library(lme4) # for lmer
library(lmerTest) # for lmer p values based on degrees of freedom
library(DHARMa)        # simulation-based residual checks (very good for mixed models)
library(performance)


f_t_dat_lo19.21 <- read.csv("data/outputs/combined-temp-pheno-dat/leaf-predictors.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

f_t_dat_lo19.21 <- f_t_dat_lo19.21 %>% 
  dplyr::rename(Tree = SSS.tag_as, Year = year)

# preapare gounping variables
# make site a factor
f_t_dat_lo19.21$Site <- as.factor(f_t_dat_lo19.21$Site) 
f_t_dat_lo19.21$Year <- as.factor(f_t_dat_lo19.21$Year)

# YEAR SHOWED no variation as a random effect, so dropped
# # temp NO REML , use maximum likihood (ML)
# lo.mixed.tl<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~  average_minTdep_l + (1 | Year) + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree) , REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
# lo.mixed.tl
# summary(lo.mixed.tl)

# temp WITH YEAR  , use maximum likihood (ML)
lo.mixed.tl<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~  average_minTdep_l + (1| Year) + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree) , REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
lo.mixed.tl
summary(lo.mixed.tl)
# temp NO REML , use maximum likihood (ML)
lo.mixed.tl<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~  average_minTdep_l + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree) , REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
lo.mixed.tl
summary(lo.mixed.tl)

# see slope. The estimate is the Slope, which is the average change in the dependent variable (leaf open) for every one unit increase in the independent variable (temp). So for every 1 degree increase in average temp departure, leaf burst is 3.17 days earlier. 

VarCorr(lo.mixed.tl)

# Residuals vs fitted — look for no pattern, constant spread
plot(lo.mixed.tl)

# Q-Q plot of residuals — check normality - some S tailed a bit
qqnorm(resid(lo.mixed.tl)); qqline(resid(lo.mixed.tl))

# Use dharma to simulate residuals
sim_res.l <- simulateResiduals(lo.mixed.tl, allow.new.levels = TRUE)
plot(sim_res.l)

# Specific tests
testDispersion(sim_res.l)
testOutliers(sim_res.l) #significant. We should Test if dropping the outliers and see if we get a similare result


# can calculate the proportion of total variance attributable to each grouping level, to say X % of the variation in budburst timing that isn't explained by temp is due to the differences between sites, versus 15% duue to differences between trees within a site.
vc.l <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(lo.mixed.tl))
vc.l$vcov / sum(vc.l$vcov)   # proportion of variance per component

# use performance package to calculate a marginal and conditional r2
performance::r2(lo.mixed.tl)
# Marginal R²: variance explained by fixed effects only (temperature)
#Conditional R²: variance explained by fixed + random effects together

# The gap between them tells you how much of your model's explanatory power comes from the site/tree structure versus temperature itself.


AIC(lo.mixed.tl) # lower AIC better, When you fit a linear mixed-effects model, R defaults to REML (Restricted Maximum Likelihood) estimation because it provides unbiased estimates for variance components. However, you cannot compare AIC values between models with different fixed effects if they are fitted using REML.If you are comparing models with different fixed effect structures, you must set REML = FALSE (or use Maximum Likelihood, method = "ML") in your model function
```

```{r table- leaf lmm results}
f_t_dat_lo19.21 <- read.csv("data/outputs/combined-temp-pheno-dat/leaf-predictors.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

f_t_dat_lo19.21 <- f_t_dat_lo19.21 %>% 
  dplyr::rename(Tree = SSS.tag_as, Year = year)

# preapare gounping variables
# make site a factor
f_t_dat_lo19.21$Site <- as.factor(f_t_dat_lo19.21$Site) 
f_t_dat_lo19.21$Year <- as.factor(f_t_dat_lo19.21$Year)


# install.packages("sjPlot")
library(sjPlot) # table functions

#  Year as a random effect, however no variance in leaf between year, boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') so it should be dropped
lo.mixed.1 <- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~ average_minTdep_l + (1 | Year) + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree) , data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
lo.mixed.1


# redo temp and pheno with no year in the model
lo.mixed <- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~ average_minTdep_l + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree) , data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
lo.mixed
summary(lo.mixed)
VarCorr(lo.mixed)


sjPlot::tab_model(lo.mixed.1, lo.mixed, 
                                  # 1. Custom predictor labels (must align with the order of coefficients)
  pred.labels = c("(Intercept)", "Minimum temp departure (C)"),

  # 2. Custom dependent variable label
  dv.labels = c("leaf opening","leaf opening"),
    show.aic = TRUE,

  # 3. Prevent sjPlot from trying to auto-fetch labels from data attributes
  auto.label = FALSE
)

# save this to show reviewers asking for year in the reviewer response

# final table with temp (no year) and imp surface

# example for adjusting the labels
sjPlot::tab_model(lo.mixed,
  # 1. Custom predictor labels (must align with the order of coefficients)
  pred.labels = c("(Intercept)", "minimum temp departure C"),

  # 2. Custom dependent variable label
  dv.labels = c("leaf opening"),
    show.aic = TRUE,

  # 3. Prevent sjPlot from trying to auto-fetch labels from data attributes
  auto.label = FALSE
)

```

```{r LMM flowers- temp}

library(lme4) # for lmer
library(lmerTest) # for lmer p values based on degrees of freedom
library(DHARMa)        # simulation-based residual checks (very good for mixed models)
library(performance)

# prep flower data

f_t_dat_ft19.21  <- read.csv("data/outputs/combined-temp-pheno-dat/flower-predictors.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

f_t_dat_ft19.21  <- f_t_dat_ft19.21 %>% 
  rename(Tree = SSS.tag_as, Year = year)

# preapare gounping variables
# make site a factor
f_t_dat_ft19.21$Site <- as.factor(f_t_dat_ft19.21$Site) 
f_t_dat_ft19.21$Year <- as.factor(f_t_dat_ft19.21$Year)

# fl.mixed <- lmer(y ~ x + (1 | group), data = my_data)
fl.mixed <- lmer(jul0.2_TGFT_d ~ average_minTdep_f + (1| Year) + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree), data = f_t_dat_ft19.21)

fl.mixed
summary(fl.mixed)

VarCorr(fl.mixed)

# interpretation: 
# Site variance: how much budburst timing varies between sites, after accounting for temperature. Large relative to Tree:Site → site-level factors (soil, microclimate, elevation) matter a lot.
 # in our case, the site explains more than the tree in a site, but not a ton more after accounting for temp. 
# Tree:Site variance: how much individual trees differ from each other within the same site. Large relative to Site → individual tree genetics/exposure matter more than which site they're in.
# Residual variance: leftover variation not explained by site, tree, or temperature — includes year-to-year noise, measurement error, unmeasured factors.

# Residuals vs fitted — look for no pattern, constant spread
plot(fl.mixed)

# Q-Q plot of residuals — check normality - some S tailed a bit
qqnorm(resid(fl.mixed)); qqline(resid(fl.mixed))

#  the smallest and largest observations (left-hand and right-hand sides of the QQ-plot, respectively) have an s-tail, 
# the smallest observations are smaller than you would expect from a normal distribution (i.e. the points are below the line on the QQ-plot). This means the lower tail of the data’s distribution has beenextended, relative to a normal distribution.
# the largest observations are larger than you would expect from a normal distribution (i.e. the points are above the line on the QQ-plot). This means the upper tail of the data’s distribution has beenextended, relative to a normal distribution (https://www.ucd.ie/ecomodel/resources/examplesofquantile-quantileplots/)

# Use dharma to simulate residuals
sim_res <- simulateResiduals(fl.mixed)
plot(fl.mixed)

# Specific tests
# # Test for overdispersion or underdispersion
# Simulation-based: It compares the standard deviation (or variance) of the observed scaled quantile residuals against the standard deviation of residuals generated from data simulated under the fitted model.Nonparametric: It avoids strict distributional or asymptotic assumptions by relying purely on the simulated residual distributions.Interpretation: A dispersion statistic close to 1.0 indicates proper dispersion (equidispersion), whereas values significantly greater than 1 suggest overdispersion (excess variance), and values lower than 1 suggest underdispersion. The accompanying p-value tests whether this deviation is statistically significant.

testDispersion(sim_res)
# not sig , so not over/unde dispersed


testOutliers(sim_res)
# sig outlier


# can calculate the proportion of total variance attributable to each grouping level, to say X % of the variation in budburst timing that isn't explained by temp is due to the differences between sites, versus 15% duue to differences between trees within a site.
vc.f <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fl.mixed))
vc.f$vcov / sum(vc.f$vcov)   # proportion of variance per component

# use performance package to calculate a marginal and conditional r2
performance::r2(fl.mixed)

# Marginal R²: variance explained by fixed effects only (temperature)
#Conditional R²: variance explained by fixed + random effects together

# The gap between them tells you how much of your model's explanatory power comes from the site/tree structure versus temperature itself.

AIC(fl.mixed) # lower AIC better, When you fit a linear mixed-effects model, R defaults to REML (Restricted Maximum Likelihood) estimation because it provides unbiased estimates for variance components. However, you cannot compare AIC values between models with different fixed effects if they are fitted using REML.If you are comparing models with different fixed effect structures, you must set REML = FALSE (or use Maximum Likelihood, method = "ML") in your model function
```

## Impervious surface relationship with phenology
```{r LMM leaves - imp}

library(lme4) # for lmer
library(lmerTest) # for lmer p values based on degrees of freedom
library(DHARMa)        # simulation-based residual checks (very good for mixed models)
library(performance)


f_t_dat_lo19.21 <- read.csv("data/outputs/combined-temp-pheno-dat/leaf-predictors.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

f_t_dat_lo19.21 <- f_t_dat_lo19.21 %>% 
  rename(Tree = SSS.tag_as, Year = year)

# preapare gounping variables
# make site a factor
f_t_dat_lo19.21$Site <- as.factor(f_t_dat_lo19.21$Site) 
f_t_dat_lo19.21$Year <- as.factor(f_t_dat_lo19.21$Year)

# remove wonderland, union, bas1, 
f_t_dat_lo19.21 <- f_t_dat_lo19.21 %>% 
   filter(Site != "WOND", Site != "SUMA",Site != "UNIO",Site != "BAS1") 

# YEAR and Tree and Site SHOWED no variation as a random effect, so dropped
# temp NO REML , use maximum likihood (ML)
lo.mixed.tl.1<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~  pA250  + (1 | Year) + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree) , REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
lo.mixed.tl.1
summary(lo.mixed.tl.1)


# temp NO REML , use maximum likihood (ML)
lo.mixed.tl<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~  pA250 + (1 | Site) , REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
lo.mixed.tl
summary(lo.mixed.tl)

# see slope. The estimate is the Slope, which is the average change in the dependent variable (leaf open) for every one unit increase in the independent variable (temp). So for every 1 degree increase in average temp departure, leaf burst is 3.17 days earlier. 

VarCorr(lo.mixed.tl)

# Residuals vs fitted — look for no pattern, constant spread
plot(lo.mixed.tl)

# Q-Q plot of residuals — check normality - some S tailed a bit
qqnorm(resid(lo.mixed.tl)); qqline(resid(lo.mixed.tl))

# Use dharma to simulate residuals
sim_res.l <- simulateResiduals(lo.mixed.tl, allow.new.levels = TRUE)
plot(sim_res.l)

# Specific tests
testDispersion(sim_res.l)
testOutliers(sim_res.l) #significant. We should Test if dropping the outliers and see if we get a similare result


# can calculate the proportion of total variance attributable to each grouping level, to say X % of the variation in budburst timing that isn't explained by temp is due to the differences between sites, versus 15% duue to differences between trees within a site.
vc.l <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(lo.mixed.tl))
vc.l$vcov / sum(vc.l$vcov)   # proportion of variance per component

# use performance package to calculate a marginal and conditional r2
performance::r2(lo.mixed.tl)
# Marginal R²: variance explained by fixed effects only (temperature)
#Conditional R²: variance explained by fixed + random effects together

# The gap between them tells you how much of your model's explanatory power comes from the site/tree structure versus temperature itself.


AIC(lo.mixed.tl) # lower AIC better, When you fit a linear mixed-effects model, R defaults to REML (Restricted Maximum Likelihood) estimation because it provides unbiased estimates for variance components. However, you cannot compare AIC values between models with different fixed effects if they are fitted using REML.If you are comparing models with different fixed effect structures, you must set REML = FALSE (or use Maximum Likelihood, method = "ML") in your model function
```

```{r zone LMEM leaves}
                            "Residential-high",

                           "Park"))



# remove wonderland, union, bas1,

# # ANOVA land use zone Year and tree at a site have no variation, so not including

# summary(lo.mixed.4)

# ANOVA land use zone
lo.mixed.4<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~ zone_nam_1 + (1 | Site), REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
lo.mixed.4
summary(lo.mixed.4)

## S3 method for class 'merMod'
model_performance(
  lo.mixed.4,
  metrics = "all",
  estimator = "ML",
  verbose = TRUE
)

performance_aic(lo.mixed.4, estimator = "ML")

library(sjmisc)
library(sjlabelled)

sjPlot::tab_model(lo.mixed.4,
                                  # 1. Custom predictor labels (must align with the order of coefficients)
  pred.labels = c("(Intercept)", "Business district:Park", "Business district:Res. high","Business district:Res. low","Business district:Res. med"),

  # 2. Custom dependent variable label
  dv.labels = "leaf opening",
  show.aic = TRUE,
string.ci = "CI",
  # 3. Prevent sjPlot from trying to auto-fetch labels from data attributes
  auto.label = FALSE
)


performance_aic(lo.mixed.4, estimator = "ML") # have to manually add this in

VarCorr(lo.mixed.4)

# Residuals vs fitted — look for no pattern, constant spread
plot(lo.mixed.4)

# Q-Q plot of residuals — check normality - some S tailed a bit
qqnorm(resid(lo.mixed.4)); qqline(lo.mixed.4)

# Use dharma to simulate residuals
sim_res.l <- simulateResiduals(lo.mixed.4, allow.new.levels = TRUE)
plot(sim_res.l) # The spread or dispersion of your scaled residuals differs significantly between at least one pair of groups.


# # this might be showing a more complex structure than lme can handle
#  Users often find that glmmTMB is less prone to singular fit or convergence warnings compared to lme4 under difficult data conditions. lme4 (lmer) uses REML by default for linear models, whereas glmmTMB uses Maximum Likelihood (ML) by default for all models. This can lead to slightly different AIC or log-likelihood values unless explicitly aligned. Choose glmmTMB if: You have zero-inflated data, overdispersion, custom correlation structures (autoregressive, spatial), or if lme4 throws persistent convergence errors or singular boundary warnings

# Specific tests
testDispersion(sim_res.l)
testOutliers(sim_res.l)


# can calculate the proportion of total variance attributable to each grouping level, to say X % of the variation in budburst timing that isn't explained by temp is due to the differences between sites, versus 15% duue to differences between trees within a site.
vc.l <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(lo.mixed.4))
vc.l$vcov / sum(vc.l$vcov)   # proportion of variance per component

# use performance package to calculate a marginal and conditional r2
performance::r2(lo.mixed.4)
# Marginal R²: variance explained by fixed effects only (temperature)
#Conditional R²: variance explained by fixed + random effects together

# The gap between them tells you how much of your model's explanatory power comes from the site/tree structure versus temperature itself.


AIC(lo.mixed.4) # lower AIC better, # 859



# look at the post hoc test

# install.packages("emmeans")
library(emmeans)
library(lme4)


mod.emm <- emmeans(lo.mixed.4, ~ zone_nam_1)
mod.emm
pairwise = pairs(mod.emm, simple="zone_nam_1",adjust="tukey")
pairwise

# 3. Extract the pairwise contrasts into a standard data frame
pairwise_df <- as.data.frame(pairwise)


library(gt)

pairwise_df %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Post-Hoc Pairwise Comparisons",
    subtitle = "Adjusted via Tukey's HSD method"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, SE, t.ratio),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_scientific(
    columns = p.value,
    rows = p.value < 0.001
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    contrast = "Comparison",
    estimate = "Difference",
    SE = "Std. Error",
    df = "df",
    t.ratio = "t",
    p.value = "p-value"
  )
```

```{r zone LMEM flowers}

f_t_dat_fl19.21 <- read.csv("data/outputs/combined-temp-pheno-dat/flower-predictors.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

f_t_dat_fl19.21 <- f_t_dat_fl19.21 %>% 
  rename(Tree = SSS.tag_as, Year = year)

# preapare gounping variables
# make site a factor
f_t_dat_fl19.21$Site <- as.factor(f_t_dat_fl19.21$Site) 
f_t_dat_fl19.21$Year <- as.factor(f_t_dat_fl19.21$Year)

# remove wonderland, union, bas1, 
f_t_dat_fl19.21 <- f_t_dat_fl19.21 %>% 
   filter(Site != "WOND", Site != "SUMA",Site != "UNIO",Site != "BAS1") 

# # ANOVA land use zone Year and tree at a site have no variation, so not including
# lo.mixed.4<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.5_TGLO_d ~ zone_nam_1 + (1| Year) + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site:Tree), REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_lo19.21)
# lo.mixed.4
# summary(lo.mixed.4)

# ANOVA land use zone
fl.mixed.4<- lmerTest::lmer(jul0.2_TGFT_d ~ zone_nam_1 + (1 | Year) + (1 | Site) + (1 | Site: Tree), REML =  FALSE, data = f_t_dat_fl19.21)
fl.mixed.4
summary(fl.mixed.4)

sjPlot::tab_model(fl.mixed.4,
                                  # 1. Custom predictor labels (must align with the order of coefficients)
  pred.labels = c("(Intercept)", "Zone: Buisness district: Park", "Zone: Buisness district: Res. high", "Zone: Buisness district: Res. low", "Zone: Buisness district: Res. med" ),

  # 2. Custom dependent variable label
  dv.labels = c("flower emergence"),
  show.aic = TRUE,

  # 3. Prevent sjPlot from trying to auto-fetch labels from data attributes
  auto.label = FALSE
)

VarCorr(fl.mixed.4)

# Residuals vs fitted — look for no pattern, constant spread
plot(fl.mixed.4)

# Q-Q plot of residuals — check normality - some S tailed a bit
qqnorm(resid(fl.mixed.4)); qqline(fl.mixed.4)

# Use dharma to simulate residuals
sim_res.l <- simulateResiduals(fl.mixed.4, allow.new.levels = TRUE)
plot(sim_res.l) # The spread or dispersion of your scaled residuals differs significantly between at least one pair of groups.


# # this might be showing a more complex structure than lme can handle
#  Users often find that glmmTMB is less prone to singular fit or convergence warnings compared to lme4 under difficult data conditions. lme4 (lmer) uses REML by default for linear models, whereas glmmTMB uses Maximum Likelihood (ML) by default for all models. This can lead to slightly different AIC or log-likelihood values unless explicitly aligned. Choose glmmTMB if: You have zero-inflated data, overdispersion, custom correlation structures (autoregressive, spatial), or if lme4 throws persistent convergence errors or singular boundary warnings

# Specific tests
testDispersion(sim_res.l)
testOutliers(sim_res.l)


# can calculate the proportion of total variance attributable to each grouping level, to say X % of the variation in budburst timing that isn't explained by temp is due to the differences between sites, versus 15% duue to differences between trees within a site.
vc.l <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fl.mixed.4))
vc.l$vcov / sum(vc.l$vcov)   # proportion of variance per component

# use performance package to calculate a marginal and conditional r2
performance::r2(fl.mixed.4)
# Marginal R²: variance explained by fixed effects only (temperature)
#Conditional R²: variance explained by fixed + random effects together

# The gap between them tells you how much of your model's explanatory power comes from the site/tree structure versus temperature itself.


AIC(fl.mixed.4) # lower AIC better, # 859



# look at the post hoc test

# install.packages("emmeans")
library(emmeans)
library(lme4)


mod.emm <- emmeans(fl.mixed.4, ~ zone_nam_1)
mod.emm
pairwise = pairs(mod.emm, simple="zone_nam_1",adjust="tukey")
pairwise

# 3. Extract the pairwise contrasts into a standard data frame
pairwise_df <- as.data.frame(pairwise)


library(gt)

pairwise_df %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Post-Hoc Pairwise Comparisons for leaf opening",
    subtitle = "Adjusted via Tukey's HSD method"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, SE, t.ratio),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_scientific(
    columns = p.value,
    rows = p.value < 0.001
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    contrast = "Comparison",
    estimate = "Difference",
    SE = "Std. Error",
    df = "df",
    t.ratio = "t",
    p.value = "p-value"
  )

```
